newsitem.title: USA: CSCE world sugar extends slide, ends at 4-week low.
newsitem.headline: CSCE world sugar extends slide, ends at 4-week low.

text.p: CSCE world sugar prices fell for the fifth straight day, ending just a notch above key chart support levels, dealers said.

In what was mainly a continuation of yesterday's steep decline, speculators sold into the market throughout the session. The selling pressure intensified by the day's end, though scale-down trade buying offered support at the lows into the close.
Nearby March futures fell 0.08 cent a lb, to 10.64, having traded from 10.63 to 10.77. Second-position May eased 0.09, to 10.74, and the remaining months fell 0.06 to 0.07.
An estimated 9,570 lots were exchanged on the day, well below Thursday's official tally of 28.169 lots.
March finished the week at a one-month low, 43 points below Monday's close of 11.07.
"The trend has certainly changed," said one trader, noting that March set a 10-week high of 11.12 cents only a week ago.

March deliery managed to hold above 10.61 cents, Thursday's intraday low, but unless the market saw an upturn in physical buying, traders said, the contract looked likely to retest the lows early next week.
Strong resistance was noted at 10.75 cents, where good producer selling was seen on Friday. Additional targets were pegged at 10.80 and 10.90-10.92.

Otherwise, traders displayed little reaction to news the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimated the 1996/97 stocks-use ratio at 15.6 percent, 0.1 percent above the cutoff for an extension of the sugar import quota.

If the ratio comes in at 15.5 percent or lower for any of the three annual review periods, the U.S. sugar import quota is automatically raised 200,000 tonnes above the annual 1.7 million allocation. This morning's cancellation effectively puts an additional 200,000 tonnes on the world market.
Traders said the news could add to the already bearish tone, but it had largely been factored in to prices beforehand.
"People knew it was going to be pretty close to 15.5 percent anyway," a trader said.
-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640
